The table reads from top to bottom as the history of image features. The first generation measures what human vision responds to, colors, edges, and keypoints, with rules designed by hand. Each of these features was built for one task and solves it well, but it rarely transfers to another, and perceptual features find images that look alike, not images that show the same thing. The second generation learns its features from labeled photos. Training searches a far larger space of filters than a designer could try: its first layer rediscovers edge and Gabor filters, and its last layer yields an embedding that transfers to new tasks with a few labeled examples. Its vocabulary, however, is the fixed list of training classes. The third generation learns without class labels, from captions (CLIP) or from the images themselves (DINOv2). Captions name millions of concepts and describe whole scenes, so search no longer depends on a list of labels: a system can describe each image in text and search the text, compare text queries with images in one embedding space, or compare images with images. The newer features do not make the older ones useless: exact color constraints, verifiable matches of the same object, explainability, and cost still favor the classical features.
The color space decides whether color distances make sense. Equal steps in sRGB are not equal to the eye; CIE Lab approximates perceived differences, and HSV separates the hue from the brightness.

Color histograms and moments describe which colors occur, not where or what. Bin-by-bin distances react strongly to small shifts across bin boundaries; the quadratic distance accounts for similar reference colors.

Gradients, Gabor filters, and HOG describe how intensities are arranged. SIFT finds distinctive keypoints and matches them across viewpoints with the ratio test, which makes it the tool for finding the same object, not the same category. Each hand-designed feature solves the task it was designed for, but rarely transfers to another.

A CNN trained for classification learns filters that resemble hand-designed ones in its first layer. Learned features are not bound to the designer’s assumptions, and with labeled examples they adapt to a new domain. The network’s pooled last stage is an image embedding that transfers to new tasks with a frozen backbone and a linear probe, but its distances were not trained for comparison. Encoders trained with metric learning, the image counterpart of bi-encoders for text, compare images better.

Class labels limit search to a fixed list and say nothing about how a scene is composed. Three paths go beyond labels: describe each image in text and search the text, compare texts and images in one embedding space (CLIP), and compare images with images in an embedding space trained for similarity (DINOv2 or CLIP).

CLIP and DINOv2 embeddings are the basis of image search today: one encoder pass per image, a vector index, and queries by example or by text. Similarity values and thresholds are specific to each model and query type.
